title: Cocaine blamed for death
article: Tamer Sayed Roha was racked by screaming fits, banged on doors and attempted to bite a police officer before succumbing to a drug- induced condition known as excited delirium.

"I knew right away he was in considerable distress," said Const. Paul Ralston of the Calgary Police Service, who last year responded to a Calgary hotel where there were reports of a man acting oddly and disturbing other guests.
"He was crouching in the corner and yelping very loud," was Ralston's first observation. "His pupils were noticeable across the room. They were huge."
Roha's behaviour and the manner in which he was treated by police prior to his death on Sept. 4, 2002, are the focus of a fatality inquiry that started Tuesday.
Roha, 27, suddenly stopped breathing shortly after police handcuffed him. Efforts to revive him failed and the man was declared dead at Foothills Hospital.
Other officers who arrived at the Quality Inn on Banff Trail N.W. said Roha was a "textbook case" of excited delirium, in which a person is markedly agitated and combative due to drug misuse.
The officers made the decision to restrain Roha.
"It was for his own safety," Ralston said. "I remember he was struggling so much, it sounded like the bones were breaking in his hand and his wrists.
Medical examiner Dr. Craig Litwin told the court the cause of death was cocaine-induced excitation delirium, which he defined as profound agitation and the instability of the nervous system.
Peter Singer, deputy chief toxicologist for the medical examiner's officer, confirmed Roha had very high levels of cocaine in his system.
Roha's family members, who are representing themselves at the inquiry, asked witnesses why Roha's face, back and ankle were bruised.
Ralston said the only mark he noticed on Roha's face was the result of carpet burn, while Litwin said the bruises could be the result of struggling.

"We just need to know the truth," said the young man's uncle, Tarek Roha, outside court. "We all believe the way he was restrained inside the room and the way he was dealt with in the room had a big impact on his death."
